title: Domain III: Sourcing & Supplier Selection - CPPB Domain III: Sourcing & Supplier Selection - Negotiation Strategies - Tactics
subject: CPPB Domain III: Sourcing & Supplier Selection

questions.q: During RFP negotiations, a vendor opens the discussion by stating a software implementation fee of $500,000, which they know is extremely high. They do this so that their subsequent 'discount' to $300,000 seems generous. This psychological tactic is known as:
questions.explain: Anchoring is a cognitive bias tactic where one party sets a high initial extreme value. This 'anchor' shifts the reference point of the negotiation, making subsequent, slightly lower offers appear more reasonable.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain III: Sourcing & Supplier Selection

questions.q: An agency and a vendor engage in negotiations focusing on mutual interests rather than rigid demands. The agency needs quick delivery, and the vendor needs flexible working hours. They agree on a schedule that satisfies both without increasing cost. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Win-Win or Principled negotiation focuses on interests, generating options for mutual gain, and solving problems collaboratively rather than fighting over a fixed pie.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain III: Sourcing & Supplier Selection

questions.q: A buyer truthfully tells a vendor, 'Your proposal is fantastic, but we only have exactly $75,000 in the grant fund for this project. If you can't hit that number, we can't do the deal.' This classic negotiation tactic is known as:
questions.explain: The 'Bogey' tactic involves tying the negotiator's hands by establishing a strict, unchangeable external constraint (like a strict budget or grant limit) to compel the other party to adapt their price to that reality.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain III: Sourcing & Supplier Selection

questions.q: During a negotiation, the IT Director becomes visibly frustrated, demanding aggressive penalties for software bugs. The Procurement Officer then smoothly steps in, apologizing for the Director's temper, and offers to drop the penalty demand if the vendor reduces their hourly rate by $10. This team tactic is called:
questions.explain: Good Cop/Bad Cop relies on one team member being unreasonable or hostile (Bad Cop) to make the other member's 'compromise' offer (Good Cop) seem highly appealing and reasonable by contrast.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain III: Sourcing & Supplier Selection

questions.q: A vendor makes a counteroffer that is less than favorable. The Lead Negotiator looks at the vendor but says absolutely nothing for 60 seconds, creating extreme discomfort in the room. This negotiation tactic relies on the power of:
questions.explain: Silence is a powerful tactic. People naturally hate uncomfortable silences and will often continue talking or begin bidding against themselves, offering premature concessions just to fill the quiet.
